articles.title: Ouvia: A User-centered Framework for Measuring Usability of Speech Translation in Real-World Communication Scenarios
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06177v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speech translation (ST) is increasingly adopted in user applications, yet its evaluation largely focuses on decontextualized testbeds and holistic quality, rather than end users' communication needs. We introduce Ouvia, an evaluation framework for measuring user-perceived usability of speech translation outputs in real-world settings. Ouvia focuses on one-to-one communication: an English speaker needs to convey a request to a Portuguese speaker, and the message is automatically translated. Through a custom web app and multi-phase study design, we collect more than 1,750 such interactions in healthcare and everyday situations, mediated by four ST systems, involving speakers from three English dialects and two genders. We find that modern ST serves people only to a limited extent---only around half of interactions are rated as usable---with significant gaps in reported usability across demographic groups. Moreover, among quality metrics, we find that QA-based evaluation is a substantially stronger predictor of real-world usability than standard approaches. Together, these findings stress the importance of situated, user-centered evaluation frameworks that go beyond holistic quality scores and attend to who the technology serves---and how well.

articles.title: Explain Like I'm 5 or Whatever I Choose: Evaluating the Potential for Interactive Complexity in Language Model Responses
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06788v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Given the increased use of large language models (LLMs) for reading and seeking information and the varying needs and backgrounds of users, direct manipulation of text can be a valuable mechanism for end-user control. However, enabling direct manipulation requires that models generate text consistent with user-requested changes. We focus on one such setting, manipulating the complexity of scientific information, and ask if models can generate multiple summaries along a continuum of text complexity that enable effective user selection and control. Through a within-subjects user study, we identify reliable complexity measures and a criterion for how models should conform to these measures. We evaluate five LLMs of different families, sizes, and reasoning abilities on $557$ scientific queries. We find that while models can vary complexity across responses, most changes remain inconsistent, with models shifting the complexity measures in the correct direction at most $33.67$% of the time.

articles.title: When More Documents Hurt RAG: Measuring and Reducing Vector Search Dilution with Domain-Scoped Retrieval
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.11350v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) degrades when applied to large, heterogeneous document collections. In RAG systems, dense similarity becomes less discriminative, causing top-$k$ retrieval to return semantically similar but contextually incorrect chunks. We refer to this failure mode as vector search dilution. Even under hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, we first observed it in a deployed Wyoming Department of Transportation (WYDOT) system; in a controlled experiment, growing the corpus from 54 to 1,128 documents cut precision@10 by 63% and recall of the answer-bearing document by 23%. Similar patterns were observed in six other DOTs. To diagnose this issue, we introduce MASDR-RAG (Metadata-Scoped Domain Retrieval for RAG) as a controlled testbed over 200 human-validated queries, five LLM backbones, six public benchmark corpora, and two index stacks. In MASDR-RAG, domain scoping is the load-bearing component. We found hard partitioning to be unsafe, whereas training-free soft scoping is safe when the scope structure is real. Furthermore, we can discover these scopes without hand-curated metadata. However, multi-agent orchestration triggers a precision-faithfulness paradox that survives format controls, prompt controls, and blind human evaluation. Based on these varied outcomes, our practical recommendation is simple: soft-scope first, then perform a single synthesis call.

articles.title: ProReviewer: Evidence-Driven Investigation for Scientific Peer Review
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.13349v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Effective peer review requires adaptive investigation that responds to evidence emerging from each paper. Existing LLM-based reviewers largely organize the review process around predefined workflows, leaving limited scope for emerging evidence to reshape investigation. We propose ProReviewer, an evidence-driven review agent that formulates reviewing as a Markov Decision Process, with a structured review log forming the core of its state. At each step, the agent uses accumulated findings to decide what to inspect next and when to conclude. As new evidence emerges, it updates the log by revising claim statuses, resolving open questions, and recording new findings. Each point in the final review cites supporting log entries, making its judgments traceable to the recorded evidence. On 1,000 held-out ICLR 2026 papers, the trained 8B ProReviewer achieves the highest average score among all compared methods, including those built on a 397B model; human evaluators prefer its reviews over all baselines on three of four review-quality dimensions.

articles.title: HiMPO: Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization for Less-Entangled Credit in Long-Horizon Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.16285v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-horizon agents compress interaction histories into memory, but final outcomes entangle memory-writing credit with tool failures and reasoning errors. We propose HiMPO, a Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization framework that supplements trajectory-level reinforcement learning with memory-specific credit. For each update, HiMPO compares the target answer's log-likelihood under the previous and updated memories while holding the remaining pre-write context fixed. A soft gate based on group-relative hindsight relevance then weights the local utility advantage. Trajectory-level credit applies to all generated tokens; memory tokens additionally receive the auxiliary advantage. Across judge-based open-domain tasks and objective compressive-memory QA, HiMPO improves task performance while preserving compressed-context efficiency. On Local Wiki Search, it improves average F1 and exact match over MemPO by 2.6 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Controlled interventions and live memory-reversion studies provide evidence of reduced blame leakage and alignment between memory credit and behavioral effects. With the policy fixed, the credit estimator remains robust to the tested forms of target noise.

articles.title: DEEPRUBRIC: Evidence-Tree Rubric Supervision for Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Deep Research Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.17029v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep research agents synthesize long-form reports by searching and reasoning over retrieved evidence. Reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards improves these agents by optimizing them against checkable criteria that translate report quality into reward signals, but its efficiency depends on whether those criteria reliably capture the task scope and evidence needs. Most existing studies ask an LLM to generate rubrics for a given query, but when the model fails to infer the underlying information needs, the generated rubrics may be incomplete and reduce RL efficiency. To obtain more reliable query--rubric supervision, we introduce DeepRubric, a data construction framework that reverses this process: instead of inferring evaluation criteria for a given query, it first determines what an evidence-backed report should be evaluated on and then synthesizes aligned query--rubric pairs from those evaluation targets. Starting from a sampled seed topic, DeepRubric builds an evidence tree by recursively expanding evidence-backed sub-questions, whose leaves serve as atomic and verifiable evaluation targets. It then uses the evidence tree to synthesize the training query and rubrics, ensuring that the reward evaluates exactly the information requested by the query. Using DeepRubric, we construct 9K query--rubric supervision examples and train DeepRubric-8B with rubric-based GRPO, achieving comparable performance to prior open state-of-the-art deep research models across three benchmarks with roughly 13x fewer RL GPU-hours.

articles.title: Confidently Wrong: Detecting Hallucinations in Financial Question Answering from LLM Internal States
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.11414v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in financial applications fail most consequentially when they are confidently wrong. Hedged, uncertain answers invite scrutiny, whereas confident errors silently degrade downstream decisions without warning. We ask how reliably such confidently wrong answers, or confident hallucinations, can be detected from a model's internal activations, and whether those activations carry information beyond its output-level confidence signals. We train linear probes on the residual stream and evaluate them on two established numerical question-answering (QA) benchmarks built from real filings, FinQA and TAT-QA. Behavioral confidence is measured as the agreement among eight resampled answers to the same question, and probe effectiveness is compared against baselines, such as token log-probabilities and the model's own True/False self-assessment of its answer. Our findings show that among confident answers, those for which all eight resamples agree, 15-23% are wrong on FinQA. There the probes have a significant advantage over output-level baselines in detecting hallucinations, holding 0.68-0.77 AUROC while the best baselines fall to 0.55-0.63, across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Our results suggest that probing can be a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control procedures in high-stakes financial applications. Code and data are available at https://github.com/richardzhewang/confidently-wrong.

articles.title: Every Time I Hire a Linguist, Inference Costs Go Down: On Linguistic Rules as Effective Prompt Compressors
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.25335v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prompt compression shortens LLM input to reduce inference cost, yet existing methods score token importance through LM forward passes. It remains questionable whether such nuanced, costly token selection is necessary. Compression requires identifying informative content, a problem that linguistic research has long addressed through cues that can be operationalized as deterministic rules. We therefore ask: can \textbf{linguistic rules alone} serve as effective prompt compressors, without LM-based scoring at compression time?
  To address this, we conduct offline evolutionary search over lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse seeds to find competitive rule combinations. The resulting linguistic compressor requires no LM forward pass at deployment and uses only CPU-side processing for compression. We evaluate it with a dual-path protocol to balance compression quality and reconstruction fidelity.
  Across short passages, multi-document reasoning, and dialogue-memory QA datasets, evolved compressors achieve performance similar to that of recent advanced prompt-compression strategies. Performance is strongest under light-to-moderate compression and degrades as compression becomes more aggressive, while the Direct and Reconstruction paths exhibit distinct patterns. Evolutionary analysis reveals that effective compression fuses signals across linguistic levels and, as the compression ratio increases, rules shift from token pruning to sentence extraction.

articles.title: Commit Locally, Exit Globally: Coordinating Adaptive Sampling and Early Exit in Diffusion Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.28166v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion language models predict tokens in parallel but still require many iterative forward passes. Adaptive sampling accelerates local token commitment, while recent global stopping methods seek to end generation early. Our trajectory analysis shows that short answers can stabilize early in decoding, whereas reasoning outputs often require more steps to settle. A fixed progress threshold therefore struggles to avoid both redundant computation on short-answer tasks and premature termination on reasoning tasks. We introduce C$^4$, a training-free framework that combines local decoding acceleration with adaptive global early exit. Confidence-Verified Early Exit (CVEE) determines when to end generation, skipping the remaining steps once its stopping criterion is met. It combines confidence and temporal agreement to adapt stopping to the observed revision history. Commit-Core-Then-Confirm (CCTC) accelerates token commitment while generation continues, reducing the decoding steps needed to complete each block. It extends confidence-threshold parallel decoding with a boundary-anchored core and one-step confirmation of deferred predictions, constraining additional commitments to mitigate premature freezing under unresolved context. With CVEE calibrated once on LLaDA, the same numerical settings transfer across all 12 zero-shot tasks and to Dream without recalibration. Under this configuration, C$^4$ reduces decoding steps by 64-95% and achieves measured decoding-loop speedups of 2.6x-18.6x, with task performance close to full decoding. Component analyses show complementary contributions: early exit supplies most savings on short-answer tasks, while local acceleration contributes more on reasoning and code generation.

articles.title: IACM-RL: Intent-Aware Context Management and Reinforcement Learning for Complex Tool Invocation under Dynamic Intent Fluctuations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.02110v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Executing long-horizon tool invocations in real-world environments is severely challenged by dynamic user intent noise. Existing methods attempt robustness via implicit history scanning or text compression, yet predominantly assume perfect instructions in simplistic scenarios. Inevitably, under fluctuating contexts, obsolete constraints dilute model attention, triggering intent deviation and repetitive API loops. To resolve this, we propose IACM-RL, a comprehensive framework for robust tool invocation. First, we introduce the DynamicIntent pipeline, synthesizing trajectories across several fine-grained fluctuation scenarios, paired with a five-dimensional diagnostic metric suite. Second, IACM-RL deploys a BeliefState-based Self-Generated Context Manager that proactively tracks shifting goals and isolates overwritten parameters using structural stale flags. To autonomously internalize this state-tracking capability, we optimize the policy using a hierarchical intent-driven reward alongside two auxiliary losses (CM extraction and state distillation). Experiments on DynamicIntent, BFCL-V3, and $\mathrm{\tau}^2$-Bench demonstrate that IACM-RL outperforms baselines, reducing infinite loops and stale context errors while enhancing out-of-domain generalization.

articles.title: ANCHOR-RE: An Agentic Biomedical Relation Extraction Framework with Retrieval Augmentation and Error-Driven Verification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.03154v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Biomedical relation extraction (BioRE) supports knowledge graph construction and hypothesis generation. In real-world settings, most candidate entity pairs are unrelated. Symbolic systems such as SemRep offer high precision and interpretability but limited recall, whereas large language models (LLMs) can produce false-positive relations. We developed ANCHOR-RE, an agentic framework that combines retrieved demonstrations, ontology-guided semantic constraints, external biomedical knowledge, and error-driven verification to improve BioRE reliability without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluated ANCHOR-RE on SemRepGS, DDI, and ChemProt using proprietary and open-weight LLMs. To assess generalizability while reducing potential pretraining contamination, we also conducted a post-cutoff temporal precision evaluation using 100 biomedical articles published in 2026. With the proprietary backbone, ANCHOR-RE improved micro-F1 over direct prompting from 0.654 to 0.676 on SemRepGS, from 0.769 to 0.881 on DDI, and from 0.937 to 0.941 on ChemProt, outperforming previously reported inference-only methods on DDI and ChemProt. Gains were also observed with the open-weight backbone. Additional experiments demonstrated cross-family model compatibility and sensitivity to external knowledge quality. Manual assessment of 500 randomly sampled positive predictions from the post-cutoff set yielded 69% precision. These results show that contextual evidence and error-driven verification can improve BioRE reliability across benchmarks, model families, and newly published literature, supporting ANCHOR-RE as a practical training-free approach to biomedical literature mining.

articles.title: Off-the-Shelf Language-Vision Encoders Predict Human Gaze Preferences in Visual World Experiments
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.07282v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A central question for computational psycholinguistics is to what extent neural language models can serve as cognitively adequate models of human language processing. However, work has been overwhelmingly focused on the unimodal case of written or spoken language. In contrast, multimodal paradigms, like visual world experiments that present participants with both visual and linguistic input simultaneously, have been neglected. In this paper, we present a novel approach that predicts patterns of gaze preferences in visual world studies. To do so, it derives target preferences by applying an attribution method to a simple bi-modal CLIP bi-encoder. We demonstrate the ability of this approach to qualitatively replicate the gaze patterns found in a seminal English visual world study demonstrating human predictive processing. It does so without a generative architecture and without the need for fine-tuning, despite not being trained for the task.

articles.title: PERCEPT: A Corpus for POS Tagging and Analysis of Persian-English Code-Mixing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.10109v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Social media has become a major venue for multilingual communication, where users frequently mix multiple languages within a single utterance. Although code-mixed corpora have been developed for several language pairs, Persian-English code-mixing remains relatively underexplored. Existing Persian resources lack Universal Dependencies (UD) part-of-speech (POS) annotations for code-mixed words, limiting both linguistic analyses and the development of syntax-aware NLP models. To address this gap, we introduce PERCEPT, the first publicly available large-scale Persian-English code-mixed corpus annotated with Universal Dependencies POS tags for code-mixed words. The dataset comprises 6,800 posts collected from Twitter (X), Instagram, and Digikala, each containing at least one identified Persian-English code-mixed word. We further present an LLM-assisted annotation framework that automatically assigns POS tags and document-level topics. Human evaluation demonstrates high agreement between the automatically generated annotations and gold annotations, confirming the reliability of the annotations. Using PERCEPT, we conduct the first comprehensive linguistic analysis of Persian-English code-mixing across multiple social media platforms. Our analyses reveal that nouns are the predominant category for code-mixed words, while the distributions of other POS categories vary across platforms. We further find that the positional distribution of code-mixed words is remarkably consistent across platforms, whereas the triggering effect is substantially more pronounced in Digikala. PERCEPT is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/PERCEPT.

articles.title: Hybrid Gated Attention
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.11805v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Gated attention is an effective approach to mitigate attention sinks and enhance the representational capacity of attention. To further extend its effectiveness-efficiency Pareto frontier, we propose a Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA) framework that contains three types of gating strategies. Specifically, these gates leverage diverse information from multiple stages of attention, and collaboratively build element-wise/head-wise gating from multiple perspectives, capturing intra-head and cross-head information interactions. Through our hybrid gating components, HyGA could provide multi-source modulation signals, enabling more comprehensive control over information flow and improving the representational capacity of attention. We also introduce low-rank matrix decomposition and learnable attention sink to further enhance training efficiency and stability. In experiments, we evaluate HyGA on widely-used benchmarks based on different backbones. The experimental results show that our HyGA comprehensively improves both training loss and various downstream performances compared with Gated attention. HyGA has also been verified to achieve the best performance at different computation costs, with comprehensive model analyses for better understanding. The proposed HyGA sheds light on a more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanism.

articles.title: LycheeMemory V2: Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents via Semantic Segment-Level Consolidation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.12990v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents must preserve information from past interactions to support future tasks. Existing memory systems typically rely on eager consolidation, invoking LLMs after each interaction to extract, summarize, or update memories. This design makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization can reduce construction cost but risks discarding fine-grained contextual evidence, whereas larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning shift the overhead to query time. We present LycheeMemory V2, an efficient long-term memory framework that replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation. Instead of consolidating every interaction, LycheeMemory batches multiple exchanges into segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection helps preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence compared with fixed-window batching. The resulting records are organized with lightweight structured indexes for query-planned evidence retrieval. Experiments using GPT-4.1-Mini show that LycheeMemory achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage. More broadly, our results suggest that the accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained, but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated.

articles.title: Refusing Intent, Not Form: Wrapper-Based Intent-Group Supervision for LLM Safety
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.13304v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A common way to improve jailbreak robustness is to train on harmful requests rewritten as role-play, translation, or other forms. When used only for harmful requests, these forms may become refusal shortcuts, weakening unseen-attack robustness and increasing benign over-refusal. We propose Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation (WIFA), which applies shared wrapper families to harmful and benign requests and groups variants by intent, encouraging decisions based on underlying intent rather than wrapper cues. WIFA supports two independent routes: WIFA-Boost prioritizes safety through two-stage training, while A-GCRT enforces consistent decisions across wrappers to mitigate over-refusal. Across three model families and two harmful training sources, both routes consistently improve safety while largely retaining capability. On Qwen--AdvBench, WIFA-Boost raises SB-avg5 from 22.1\% to 63.7\%, the best among compared methods; A-GCRT raises it to 46.7\% while reducing OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7\% to 17.4\%, unlike reproduced defenses whose safety gains increase over-refusal. Across three AdvBench-trained backbones, both routes substantially reduce ASR on 15 unseen attack families and under model-adaptive GCG and RandomSearch. Overall, WIFA provides reusable intent-group supervision across models and training sources, supporting high safety through WIFA-Boost and substantial safety gains with less unnecessary refusal through A-GCRT.

articles.title: Frozen Memory Is Not Enough: Rethinking External Memory as Extraction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.17050v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Methods for improving knowledge use in large language models typically fall into two regimes. Non-parametric retrieval offers flexible access to external knowledge, but adds retrieval latency, context overhead, and only shallow integration with the backbone. Parametric adaptation is efficient at inference time, but entangles knowledge with model weights and can be hard to update, audit, or transfer. Engram-style hashed memory occupies a middle regime: it stores learned information in an external, addressable table, yet consumes that table through a small learned reader. This raises a basic question: when such a memory is moved across backbones, what matters more, the frozen memory itself or the target-side reader? We study this question through cross-model frozen-memory extraction, in which a memory trained on a source model is frozen and attached to a different target model, with only a lightweight reader trained. Ablations show that learned memory content and correct addressing both matter, but the transferred table becomes useful only through a reader aligned to the target model. In downstream question answering tasks, a dual-layer, four-branch reader nearly closes the gap between same-model and cross-model reuse, achieving an average score of 38.8 under our controlled evaluation protocol. Moreover, when the provider reader is directly compatible with the target interface, the frozen artifact can provide substantial utility without target-side training, while optional reader adaptation yields further improvement. These results suggest that Engram can serve as a reusable external knowledge artifact, provided that the target has access to a compatible reader interface; target-side adaptation can further improve alignment when direct reader reuse is insufficient.

articles.title: DCGC: Draft-Conditioned Global Correction for Complex Reasoning with Masked Diffusion Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.25428v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Correcting flawed reasoning traces remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs), whose autoregressive generation can propagate early mistakes into subsequent reasoning. We introduce DCGC, a Masked Diffusion Model (MDM) framework for global correction that uses an imperfect solution draft from an upstream solver as auxiliary context. DCGC combines task-specific Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a novel inference-time mechanism called Dynamic Dual-CFG. This mechanism separates problem-only and joint problem-draft branches and scales the draft-conditioned residual using a relative confidence gap. Across math, code, and knowledge reasoning benchmarks, DCGC outperforms standard sampling and simpler CFG variants, with additional results suggesting transfer to different diffusion backbones. In test-time setting where ground-truth failure labels are unavailable, DCGC improves full test set accuracy by correcting low-consensus upstream outputs, highlighting its utility as a verifier-free global correction module for difficult reasoning instances.

articles.title: TreeGraft: Adaptive Multi-Drafter Grafting for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.26112v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through a draft-then-verify paradigm. Building on this, tree-structured methods improve inference by organizing proposals into multiple candidate paths, increasing the accepted length. However, existing tree-structured methods use a single drafter for all drafting steps, creating a dilemma: a smaller drafter is fast but yields lower-quality trees, whereas a larger drafter improves tree quality but suffers from high latency. To address this, we propose TreeGraft, a multi-drafter framework in which drafters of different costs jointly construct a shared draft tree. TreeGraft uses the stronger drafter to rescore candidates by updating scores assigned by the weaker drafter, reselect grafting positions, and recover promising paths left unexplored. It also integrates stronger drafter expansions non-destructively, preserving existing branches that may still be accepted by the target model. Together, these designs improve the quality of the shared draft tree. To control the drafting cost, TreeGraft introduces a lightweight scheduler distilled from an offline value system to decide when to call the stronger drafter. Across 10 model pairs and 6 benchmarks, TreeGraft outperforms the better of the two fixed single-drafter endpoint strategies by 15.1% on average, reaching a maximum gain of 26.6%. Our code is available at https://github.com/fjm9933/TreeGraft.

articles.title: BTS-AgentBench: A Deterministic, Replayable Pipeline from Read-Only Telemetry Logs to Agent Benchmarks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.27334v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Operational facilities accumulate extensive local telemetry, but agent-ready interactive evaluations with source-verifiable answers are costly to construct from such archives. Site-specific measurement histories also motivate a local conversion workflow that can operate where raw operational data must remain under organizational control. We introduce BTS-AgentBench, a deterministic compiler that transforms read-only telemetry and equipment metadata into tool-backed, multi-turn agent tasks, phase-level targets, evidence and executable evaluation contracts. The BTS release includes 532 episodes across nine families; a second-corpus port produces 204 XAI4HEAT episodes. Frozen-input replay reproduces released artifacts byte-for-byte, and independent raw-source checks cover all 89 BTS and 41 XAI4HEAT test episodes. Replayable provenance links 1,170 trial identities to recorded execution and scorer conditions, while 1,125 completed traces retain model responses and tool results. An obligation-level comparison of 216 scored failures found that linked records exposed additional recorded failed obligations in 202 cases (93.5\%), including tool arguments, stream identity, state carryover and missing interaction steps. The pipeline thereby supports source-grounded task generation, exact reconstruction and auditable diagnosis of agent executions. Code, released benchmarks, and reproduction instructions are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/telemetry-benchmark-reproduction-3D68

articles.title: RATIO: A Benchmark for Retrieval Across Typed Ideation Operations in Scientific Literature
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.27394v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieved scientific literature can serve as inspiration for both human and AI scientists. Inspiration can take different forms: prior work may directly suggest how to address a problem, or surface directions at different levels of abstraction---zooming out to a more general view or zooming in to a concrete realization. We introduce RATIO (Retrieval Across Typed Ideation Operations), a large-scale benchmark in which relevance is defined by three operations which we name ideation moves: Address retrieves potential approaches for stated problems, Broaden retrieves more general formulations, and Specify retrieves concrete instantiations. RATIO is constructed from millions of full-text scientific papers across CS literature via a general recipe that extends discourse-marker distant supervision---previously used only for classification---to corpus-scale retrieval, combined with extensive LLM and human vetting. Experiments show that operation-specific fine-tuning substantially boosts retrievers and LLM reranking helps further, but much room for improvement remains. Researchers blind to condition found the fine-tuned retriever's candidates more useful as inspirations. RATIO provides a scalable training and evaluation framework for retrieval components that support literature-grounded ideation, opening up new research avenues in scientific inspiration retrieval. We release full data, code, models, and annotations.

articles.title: Lazy Grounding: Attacking Search Agents with Factual Evidence
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.30303v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Search agents mitigate hallucination by grounding their answers in retrieved web results. However, retrieval-based approaches also introduce an attack surface: agents may cite misinformation from poisoned search corpora containing false or malicious documents. We demonstrate that, in some cases, search agents' reasoning and responses may be steered by completely factual but distracting information. We refer to this failure as lazy grounding. We expose lazy grounding by injecting nearby evidence from answer-changing rewrites of benchmark questions into the search corpora. Each document contains factual evidence that supports a neighboring rewritten question but is retrieved for the original question. Across 12 model-benchmark pairs, the attack causes the accuracy of search agents' responses to drop by 5.9 points on average and by up to 17.3 points, while inducing nearby-answer adoption in every setting. The effect is even stronger when nearby evidence appears later or is more answer-shaped. Our results show that robust search agents must defend against not only misinformation but also the misapplication of factual evidence. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/frankyzha/lazy-grounding.

articles.title: DischargeBench: Pre-Deployment Evaluation of LLM Discharge Educators through Persona-Grounded Patient Simulation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.20827v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Effective discharge education is personalized: a clinician adapts the discharge plan to each patient's literacy, recall, and personality. Before large language models (LLMs) take on this role with real patients, they need to be evaluated in conversations with diverse patients, yet existing evaluations target static, artifact-generation, or question-answering tasks. We introduce **DischargeBench**, a pre-deployment benchmark in which a candidate LLM educator teaches a persona-grounded simulated patient in an open-ended, multi-turn conversation. We curate **MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench**, 320 cases across 16 ICD chapters, each paired with a patient persona that varies personality, education level, health literacy, and recall. Each conversation is scored on Conversation Quality, Topic Checklist Score (TCS), Simulated Comprehension Score (SCS), and a Claim-Level Safety Audit (CLSA) by an LLM judge validated against physician annotations. Across eight closed- and open-source LLMs, the best model scored only 0.70 on TCS and 0.72 on SCS, and distrustful and anxious patients lowered comprehension for every model. DischargeBench is intended as a screening step before human evaluation, not as evidence of readiness to educate patients.

articles.title: Reviser: Writing and Editing Text with Autoregressive Cursor Actions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.20830v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models write text once, left to right, and models that write in other orders, such as diffusion LMs, pay for it with many full-sequence passes. We introduce Reviser, a decoder-only Transformer that writes and edits text with cursor actions (insert, move, delete, stop) that a deterministic executor applies to a canvas. Reviser is autoregressive over its own actions, so a step costs the same as an autoregressive (AR) step. We train Reviser to continue text, including a self-correction recipe that types a wrong token and deletes it, and Reviser-Edit to revise a draft, and compare each with a same-size AR model trained on the same data, using three LLM judges on continuations cut to the same length. Reviser-Edit beats its matched AR rewriter on CoEdIT SARI (+7.2 at 100M, +4.5 at 300M; two seeds agree) with a third of the decoding steps and latency, though the AR rewriter corrects grammar better. In continuation, Reviser beats diffusion LMs of similar size (62-74% win rate) at a fraction of their compute; two of three judges prefer its AR twin, and one slightly prefers Reviser at 100M. Reviser fills gaps it left and backspaces a just-typed repeated token with probability 0.85-0.87.

articles.title: An Iterative LangGraph Agent for Text-to-SQL: Natural Language Access to the Chicago Crime Database
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.22917v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Non-technical stakeholders frequently cannot write the SQL needed to extract insights from operational databases. We built and evaluated a Text-to-SQL agent that closes this gap end to end: a six-node LangGraph StateGraph checks question relevance, fetches the live schema, generates PostgreSQL, validates it with a dry run, retries on failure, executes the query, and narrates the result set in plain English. The agent uses prompt engineering only; no model was fine-tuned. We evaluated it on the Chicago Crime dataset (approximately 8.5 million records, 22 attributes) against a hand-built benchmark of 100 natural language questions with ground-truth SQL, stratified into 30 Easy, 40 Medium and 30 Hard items. Comparing two prompt revisions of the same agent, the revised system (V2) reached a Valid SQL Rate of 93% (from 87%), an Execution Accuracy of 60% under a hybrid relational equivalence metric (from 47%; 19% from 12% under strict JSON matching), and a mean Synthesis Quality of 4.34 out of 5 (from 3.91). The single largest driver was removing a LIMIT 10 instruction from the system prompt, which had been truncating multi-row answers. Error analysis attributes the residual failures to relevance-checker false rejections, ambiguous question semantics, and free-tier API rate limits rather than to the language generation step. We report no comparison against an external baseline system or a public benchmark; the study is a single-model engineering evaluation.

articles.title: ARAFA: An LLM-Generated Arabic Fact-Checking Dataset
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.25833v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automatic fact-checking poses a significant challenge in Arabic natural language processing due to the scarcity of datasets and resources. In this manuscript, we introduce Arafa, a new large-scale dataset for fact-checking in Modern Standard Arabic, constructed through an automated framework leveraging large language models (LLMs). The dataset was constructed through a three-step pipeline: (1) claim generation from Arabic Wikipedia pages with supporting textual evidence, (2) claim mutation to generate challenging counterfactual claims with refuting evidence, and (3) an automatic validation step to validate that the generated claims are either supported or refuted by their accompanying evidence, or if the evidence does not provide enough information to judge the validity of the claims. The resulting dataset comprises 181,976 claim-evidence pairs labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information. Human evaluation carried out on a test sample from the dataset demonstrated strong inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.89) using Cohen's Kappa for supported claims and (kappa = 0.94) for refuted claims. Automatic validation based on a human-evaluated sample achieved 86% accuracy for supported claims and 88% for refuted ones. To showcase Arafa's value as a resource for automatic Arabic fact-checking, four open-source transformer-based models were fine-tuned using Arafa, with the top-performing model achieving a Macro F1-score of 77% on the test data. In addition to Arafa being the first large-scale dataset for Arabic fact-checking, our framework presents a scalable approach for developing similar resources for other low-resource languages.

articles.title: MemoryAthena: Adaptive Routing over Latent and Generated Memories
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.25853v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Learned-memory methods store information in an explicit table and consume it through a separate reader, allowing addressing, storage, and reading to be modified independently. We study whether useful memory can also be generated rather than only retrieved. MemoryAthena uses three pathways: direct Engram retrieval (E), generation from retrieved Engram cues (GE), and generation from causal backbone states without consulting the memory table (GH). Generated memory is conditionally useful: it can complement E in one context but interfere with it in another. MemoryAthena therefore treats E as an anchor and learns when a generated representation should intervene. With the backbone, memory, generators, and readers frozen, a lightweight causal routing head is trained from counterfactual future-token likelihood advantages of GE and GH relative to E. At inference time, an admitted candidate modifies the E residual through bounded interpolation, while rejection recovers the direct pathway exactly. On question answering, MemoryAthena raises the five-task average from 37.65 to 39.28 over the direct pathway of the same checkpoint, while the six-task general-NLP average increases from 76.73 to 79.13. The complete memory-side system contains approximately 201M parameters, excluding the frozen backbone. Further analyses show complementary strengths among E, GE, and GH across tasks and inputs. These results support generated memory as a selective correction to direct retrieval and highlight routing when, which, and how strongly to intervene as the central challenge.

articles.title: EduBehaviors: Assertion-based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.27043v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models have enabled rapid deployment of language classification and analysis, allowing users to describe complex constructs in natural language, such as pedagogical moves or expressions of learning and engagement, and label them in conversational datasets such as classroom or tutoring transcripts. However, because LLM reasoning is opaque, we have no verifiable, mechanistic insight into why a model chose a label for an utterance, and output differences over time or across models challenge replication. We introduce the EduBehaviors framework to generate interpretable, reliable, and scalable construct annotations in educational dialogue data that retain human agency while leveraging the strengths of generative AI, encoders, and machine learning models. We evaluate the framework on the TalkMoves dataset, predicting the Teacher TalkMoves labels. Our best configuration results in a macro-F1 of 0.764 and 0.756 Cohen's kappa, demonstrating improvements over direct prompting approaches and showing competitiveness with fine-tuned classifiers while gaining the benefit of greater transparency and comparability. To facilitate adoption and operationalization of the EduBehaviors framework in educational dialogue data by other researchers, we also release the EduBehaviors Toolkit with two complementary open-source tools based on the TalkMoves application.

articles.title: Policy-Conditioned AI-Use Detection: An Evidentiary Framework for Academic Publishing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38427v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Major venues now publish detailed rules about how authors, reviewers, and area chairs may use AI, and those rules differ by role, by task, and by what must be disclosed. AI detection, the instrument usually proposed to enforce them, estimates something else: whether an AI model wrote the text. We argue that this target is misaligned with the decisions conferences and journals face, and propose policy-conditioned AI-use detection, an evidentiary framework for assessing whether a human--AI workflow complied with a stated rule. Policy makes the governing rule an explicit input. Inference reports hypotheses, evidence, calibration regime, and uncertainty in place of verdicts such as "AI detected". Evaluation builds benchmarks from reproducible pipelines that generate compliant and non-compliant workflows, and reports true positive rate at a false positive rate the venue fixes in advance. We work the framework through peer review, where at plausible violation rates a detector at a strong operating point still flags more compliant authors than violating ones. The framework therefore also names what a venue must instrument: structured disclosure, approved-tool routing that respects reviewer confidentiality, and a path by which a finding can be contested. Under this framing a detector is not an authorship classifier but an auditable procedure with an error rate the venue fixes in advance and can defend.

articles.title: Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.02022v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI-based ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of their ideas, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that seemingly small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.

articles.title: Quality-Aware Self-Correcting Speech Translation on an Edge Device
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.07545v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present a fully offline speech-to-speech translation pipeline that runs on a Jetson Nano (4 GB) and corrects its own weak translations without retraining. A Whisper-tiny ASR feeds an Opus-MT translator; multilingual BERT cosine similarity acts as a Quality Estimation (QE) gate, triggering a secondary-pass when confidence falls below a pre-defined threshold $\tau$. We compare three correction methods: QE reranking (M1), Minimum Bayes-Risk decoding (M2), and constrained beam search (M3). On 1,012 FLORES-200 sentences (English-Spanish), M2 at $\tau=0.90$ produces statistically significant improvements over greedy decoding on BLEU (+0.67, p<0.001), ChrF (+0.51, p<0.001), and COMET (+0.0020 at N=3, p=0.002); M1 yields no significant gains, and M3 is significantly worse than baseline (p>0.99). Our central finding is that QE functions effectively as a gate but poorly as a ranker: removing the QE model from candidate selection (M1$\to$M2) does not hurt quality and frees 680 MB from the critical path. Using a gain-to-edit ratio adapted from the post-editing-effort literature, we further show that smaller candidate pools (N=3) yield more surgical corrections with better semantic adequacy, while larger pools (N=10) maximise lexical reward. We release the system and demonstrate live translation across six language pairs.

articles.title: Monte Carlo Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.07643v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most KV-cache eviction methods ask, in effect, which memory appeared important while reading the prompt? We instead ask which memory will matter while answering? Since decoding queries are unavailable at eviction time, prior future-aware methods rely on pseudo-responses or synthetic future-query estimates. We cast fixed-budget future-aware eviction as distributional estimation over plausible model-conditional query trajectories and introduce LORE-KV (Lookahead Output-perturbation with Reliability-weighted Ensembles for Key-Value caches), a training-free method that samples short autoregressive continuations from the frozen target model and uses their response-side query states to estimate prompt-token utility. Tokens are scored by projected leave-one-out attention-output deletion cost and aggregated across sampled futures with optional trajectory weighting. The temporary continuations are discarded before final decoding, requiring no auxiliary model or training. Ablations isolate the mechanism: at B=128, a single response-side continuation recovers about 89% of the gain over the prompt-window control, while additional futures provide smaller improvements. At B=128, LORE-KV raises the LongBench average on Qwen2.5-14B from 45.49 to 48.24 (+2.75) and the 16K RULER average on Mistral-7B from 45.20 to 51.05 (+5.85); on Llama-3.1-8B, the RULER margin over AnDPro widens to +8.13 and +11.65 points at 64K and 128K contexts. Gains diminish at larger cache budgets and coexist with task-level regressions. LORE-KV incurs 1.46-2.77x AnDPro's per-sample wall-clock time as a one-time compression overhead across six dense and hybrid-attention backbones. Project webpage: https://ahsanbilal7.github.io/train_free_kv/

articles.title: ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.09396v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As text-to-SQL systems move beyond demonstrations toward real-world deployment, ambiguity in user questions becomes a primary source of errors. Such ambiguities are often subtle, domain- or data-specific, and can silently cause system outputs to deviate from the user's true intent. Ambiguity is traditionally addressed through conversational clarification, which is often inefficient, cognitively demanding, and poorly aligned with real-world user workflows. We propose structured disambiguation, a new paradigm in which ambiguity is resolved through explicit, constrained interactions rather than free-form dialogue. We construct ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL), the first text-to-SQL benchmark featuring naturally occurring, unconstrained ambiguities over real-world databases, with complete annotations of all valid ambiguity points, interpretations, and SQL queries. Experimental results show that text-to-SQL remains challenging in the presence of ambiguity: gpt-6-sol achieves only 51% end-to-end execution accuracy, and no open-source model exceeds 27%.

articles.title: ILM: An AI-Powered Storytelling Educational Tool
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.12064v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Digital technologies have made Islamic narratives more accessible, but existing platforms provide limited support for structured learning and comprehension of these stories, particularly in Arabic and multilingual settings. We present ILM, an interactive educational platform for Stories of the Prophets that combines Arabic natural language processing, structured knowledge representation, and retrieval-based question generation. Admin-approved Arabic narratives are processed by a Knowledge Graph (KG) Constructor Engine that identifies entities and narrative relationships and stores them as structured knowledge, enabling learners to explore stories through a visual story map and answer entity- and relation-based questions generated from the KG. Separately, a multilingual retrieval pipeline retrieves relevant passages from the original narratives to generate multiple-choice and open-ended comprehension questions. For open-ended questions, an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluates learners' answers against the retrieved passages and reference answers to determine correctness. The platform also incorporates Quranic content as a separate enrichment layer, allowing selected narratives to be supplemented with source-supported information. By combining structured knowledge with passage-based retrieval, ILM supports narrative exploration, comprehension, and assessment across Arabic and multilingual content. The system demonstrates the feasibility of combining structured knowledge representation and retrieval-based generation to support interactive learning of Islamic narratives. A demo is available at anonymous.4open.science/r/mml-5FCF.

articles.title: HarnessSQL: Harness-Native Training for SQL Agents in Realistic Database Environments
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.12274v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Text-to-SQL models are commonly trained to map questions directly to static queries, whereas real-world database agents operate through stateful, multi-turn interaction with live databases -- inspecting schemas, executing probe queries, diagnosing errors, and revising hypotheses. This creates a critical train-deploy mismatch, as the execution harness that mediates this interaction is introduced only at inference time. To bridge this gap, we propose HarnessSQL, a harness-native post-training framework that preserves the full interaction structure throughout both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. HarnessSQL builds isolated, executable database environments paired with hidden execution oracles, rolls out teachers directly inside the target SQL harness, and retains only verified trajectories for full-sequence SFT, followed by execution-reward RL. Across Spider 2.0-SQLite, HarnessSQL dramatically boosts the execution accuracy of compact models, raising Qwen3-8B from 15.5% to 45.2% and Qwen3-14B from 22.2% to 54.8%, while transferring effectively to out-of-distribution interactive benchmarks such as BIRD-Interact and LiveSQLBench. Our findings demonstrate that training database agents directly within their execution harness is essential for mastering complex, long-horizon database workflows.

articles.title: From Structure to Validity: Mechanism-Guided Generation and Refinement of LLM Rubrics
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.13375v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Rubrics have been widely used to evaluate and optimize language models on open-ended tasks. However, existing work primarily focuses on generating better rubrics, with limited understanding of what makes rubric design effective. In this work, we conduct a systematic mechanistic analysis of rubric design across criterion organization, criterion operationalization, and score aggregation. Our analysis shows that structural organization enables more comprehensive criterion construction, semantic specification alone does not ensure effective criterion-level judgments, and sophisticated score aggregation provides limited additional gains. Guided by these findings, we introduce Adaptive Rubric Tree Search with Hybrid refinement (ARTS-Hybrid), which combines adaptive tree construction with semantic-first, response-calibrated refinement. Experiments across benchmarks show that ARTS-Hybrid improves both end-to-end evaluation performance and intrinsic rubric quality. Further experiments suggest that, beyond evaluation, rubrics generated by ARTS-Hybrid provide effective signals for model optimization.

articles.title: Evaluating LLMs as Agentic Workflow Executors in Real-World Customer Support Skills
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.14346v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Enterprise customer-support agents increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute bounded, tool-using workflows. We study this problem through the lens of Skill LLMs: specialized executors that operate within a selected skill context and must complete a narrow, stateful workflow under policy and tool constraints. We present a benchmark construction pipeline that mines recurrent workflows from real-world transcripts, converts them into structured skill descriptions, maps them to tool requirements, simulates environment state with Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible mocks, and generates multi-turn tool-using dialogues. Using this benchmark, we conduct a large-scale zero-shot evaluation of 17 language models spanning closed model families and deployment-oriented open-weight models from 1.7B to 14B parameters, each judged independently by five strong LLM judges, plus a deterministic rule-based evaluator that checks tool coverage, hallucinated tool use, and unsupported claims. We find a consistent ranking in which GPT-5.4 leads by a wide margin and QWEN3.5-9B is the strongest open-weight model (below 20B), outperforming several closed baselines under every judge. We also find that judge choice is not a negligible methodological detail: pairwise judge agreement on the pass/fail verdict averages Kappa=0.524 across 10 judge pairs. These results suggest that comprehensive zero-shot evaluation of skill execution requires judge reliability as carefully as model capability.

articles.title: Learning Proposition-Level Links from Sentence-Level Supervision for Neuro-Symbolic NLI
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.15158v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study neuro-symbolic natural language inference (NLI) with independently translated propositional representations of the premise and hypothesis. Before symbolic reasoning, the system must infer semantic links between their proposition-level units (atoms). Existing systems based on Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) identify these links using fixed embedding-based source selection and pretrained sentence-level NLI models not trained for atom-level linking. We introduce a trainable atom linker that jointly predicts link existence, source selection, and relation type. Without atom-pair training annotations, we treat cross-formula link structures as latent and train the linker from sentence-level NLI labels, keeping the translator and SAT reasoner fixed. We evaluate on the full public test splits of Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) and Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge (SICK), and the matched and mismatched validation splits of Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI). Our system improves accuracy by 11.40-27.09 percentage points over a baseline applying sentence-trained NLI models unchanged to atom pairs within the same SAT pipeline. It also improves over the prior fixed-linker AMR-to-SAT system by 8.14-26.32 percentage points on SNLI and both MNLI splits, with a smaller gain on SICK.

articles.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.15692v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

articles.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.15897v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.

articles.title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.16859v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

articles.title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.18818v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

articles.title: Prompt Stability Matters: Evaluating and Optimizing Auto-Generated Prompt in General-Purpose Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.13546v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automatic prompt generation plays a crucial role in enabling general-purpose multi-agent systems to perform diverse tasks autonomously. Existing methods typically evaluate prompts based on their immediate task performance, overlooking the intrinsic qualities that determine their reliability. This outcome-centric view not only limits interpretability but also fails to account for the inherent stochasticity of large language models (LLMs). In this work, we bring attention to prompt stability-the consistency of model responses across repeated executions-as a key factor for building robust and effective prompt generation systems. To quantify this, we propose semantic stability as a criterion for assessing the response consistency of prompts. Based on the proposed metric, we developed the first stability-aware general-purpose prompt generation system that leverages stability feedback to iteratively enhance both prompt quality and system-level performance. Furthermore, we establish a logical chain between prompt stability and task success by analyzing the structural dependencies within our system, proving stability as a necessary condition for effective system-level execution. Empirical results across general and domain-specific tasks demonstrate that our stability-aware framework improves both accuracy and output consistency. By shifting the focus from one-off results to persistent reliability, our work offers a new perspective on prompt design and contributes practical tools for building more trustworthy general-purpose systems. The UI and source code for our system are publicly available at: https://xucheng63.github.io/MyDataPilot/.

articles.title: The Invisible Leash: Why RLVR May or May Not Escape Its Origin
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.14843v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances highlight Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) as a promising approach to enhancing LLM capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether the current practice of RLVR truly expands models' reasoning boundary or mainly amplifies high-reward outputs that base models already know. We introduce empirical support dynamics, a framework that quantifies how RLVR preserves, expands, and shrinks access to verified solutions. Applied across models, reasoning tasks, and training checkpoints, it matches verified successes question by question to reveal changes that aggregate accuracy can conceal. Across the evaluated model-level benchmark aggregates, \textit{the shrinkage of observed support outweighs its expansion}: more questions lose a verified success than gain one at the stated sampling budgets. These losses occur alongside gains in \texttt{pass@1}. Some RLVR models increase average token-level entropy while reducing final-answer entropy: their token choices become more uncertain on average even as their final answers become more concentrated. Together, these findings reveal an ``invisible leash'' in current RLVR practice: it can make existing successes more reliable while losing access to other verified solutions. Empirical support dynamics make this imbalance measurable and motivate exploration strategies that reach underrepresented solutions while retaining prior successes.

articles.title: Ground-Truth Subgraphs for Better Training and Evaluation of Knowledge Graph Augmented LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.04473v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Retrieval of information from graph-structured knowledge bases represents a promising direction for improving the factuality of LLMs. While various solutions have been proposed, a comparison of methods is difficult due to the lack of challenging QA datasets with ground-truth targets for graph retrieval. We present SynthKGQA, an LLM-powered framework for generating high-quality Knowledge Graph Question Answering datasets from any Knowledge Graph, providing the full set of ground-truth facts in the KG to reason over questions. To demonstrate its utility, we apply SynthKGQA to ogbl-wikikg2, a Wikidata-derived KG, and validate generated items against an up-to-date dump of Wikidata to create GTSQA. This new dataset is specifically designed to test zero-shot generalization with respect to unseen graph structures and relation types, enabling us to analyze the abilities and limitations of SOTA graph retrieval approaches at an unprecedented level of granularity. We also show that KG retrievers trained on GTSQA can transfer to a human-curated benchmark, and that the ground-truth subgraphs produced by SynthKGQA provide a better training supervision signal than previously-used heuristics.

articles.title: The Instability of Safety: How Random Seeds and Temperature Expose Inconsistent LLM Refusal Behavior
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.12066v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Current safety evaluations of large language models rely on single-shot testing, implicitly assuming that model responses are deterministic and representative of the model's safety alignment. We challenge this assumption by investigating the stability of safety refusal decisions across random seeds and temperature settings. Testing four instruction-tuned models from three families (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Qwen 3 8B, Gemma 3 12B) on 876 harmful prompts across 20 sampling configurations (4 temperatures x 5 seeds), we find that 18-28% of prompts exhibit decision flips (the REFUSE/PARTIAL/COMPLY label changes across configurations), depending on the model. Our Safety Stability Index (SSI) reveals that higher temperatures significantly reduce decision stability (Friedman chi-squared = 396.81, p < 0.001), with mean within-temperature SSI dropping from 0.977 at temperature 0.0 to 0.942 at temperature 1.0. We validate findings across all model families using Claude 3.5 Haiku as a unified external judge, achieving 89.1% inter-judge agreement with the Llama 70B judge on the two models both judges labeled (Cohen's kappa = 0.62). Within each model, prompts with higher compliance rates exhibit lower stability (Spearman rho = -0.47 to -0.70, all p < 0.001), indicating that models "waver" more on borderline requests. These findings demonstrate that single-shot safety evaluations are insufficient for reliable safety assessment and that evaluation protocols must account for stochastic variation in model behavior. For Llama 3.1 8B, single-shot evaluation agrees with multi-sample ground truth only 92.5% of the time when pooling across temperatures (98.7% at greedy to 90.3% at temperature 1.0), and we recommend scaling samples with temperature--one at greedy, three at low temperature, more at higher temperatures (where three reach only ~95%), and ten when pooling--rather than a single flat threshold.

articles.title: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Automated Reward Design
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.13399v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Crafting effective reward signals remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) for complex reasoning. Existing methods for automated reward optimization search with a fixed proposer which never learns from its costly trials. We present Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL), a dual-training framework for autonomous discovery of reward structures. An outer-loop proposer composes a reward from task primitives, and an inner policy trains with this reward. The proposer itself learns by policy gradient from the validation performance of the inner policy. Thus, DERL utilizes past-trial feedback to shape its reward-proposal distribution, an empirical meta-gradient of task success. We validate DERL on embodied (ALFWorld), scientific (ScienceWorld), and mathematical (GSM8K, MATH) reasoning. On multi-turn agent benchmarks, DERL outperforms strong baselines, significantly on out-of-distribution tasks. In mathematics, DERL improves on the outcome reward where directly added primitives hurt. Further analyses under matched compute show that our proposer effectively captures the meta-gradient to discover useful reward signals.

articles.title: SWE-Spot: Building Small Repo-Experts with Repository-Centric Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.21649v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The deployment of coding agents in privacy-sensitive and resource-constrained environments drives the demand for capable open-weight Small Language Models (SLMs). However, they suffer from a fundamental capability gap: unlike frontier large models, they lack the inference-time strong generalization to handle complicated, unfamiliar codebases. We identify that the prevailing Task-Centric Learning (TCL) approach, which scales exposure across disparate repositories, fails to address this limitation. In response, we propose Repository-Centric Learning (RCL), a shift that prioritizes vertical, single-repository depth over horizontal, single-task breadth for SLM training. To accomplish this depth, we design a four-unit Repository-Centric Experience, transforming static codebases into interactive learning signals, to train SWE-Spot-4B, a family of highly compact models built as repo-specialized experts. Under controlled comparisons with the same teacher and data budget, RCL consistently outperforms TCL across tasks, teachers, model scales, and programming languages. On seven target repositories, SWE-Spot-4B experts match or exceed existing open-weight models up to $8\times$ larger (e.g., CWM by Meta, Qwen3-Coder-30B) and surpass or match efficiency-focused commercial models (e.g., GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-nano) across multiple SWE tasks. Further analysis reveals that RCL yields higher training and inference efficiency, deep knowledge acquisition, and can scale to repository-cluster experts. Our work emphasizes that for building efficient intelligence, repository mastery is a distinct, necessary, and practical dimension that complements general coding capability.

articles.title: When Is Enough Not Enough? Illusory Completion in Search Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.07549v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In agentic search, an LLM agent searches the web, reads the pages it finds, and decides what to look for next before returning an answer. But can we trust an answer simply because the agent returns it? Often not, and even a correct answer can be a lucky guess: on questions with several constraints, we find that agents conclude the task is complete while a constraint remains unverified in up to 48% of their correct answers. We call this illusory completion. To see how it arises, we introduce the Epistemic Ledger, which tracks at every turn what the retrieved pages establish about each constraint and what the agent claims. Across 13 agents, from 7B RL-trained models to frontier LLMs, training and scale raise accuracy but change the pattern of verification failures rather than eliminating them: constraints may be left unchecked, assumed without support, or retained despite refuting evidence. To measure what agents lose without tracking their constraints, we show them each constraint's state, approximated by LiveLedger, a lightweight 4B tracker. Agents then answer 4.4-16.1 points more questions correctly, suggesting that on their own, they may not track what they have verified and what remains.

articles.title: Semantic Communities and Boundary-Spanning Lyrics in K-pop: A Graph-Based Unsupervised Analysis
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.12881v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We examine how lyric representation shapes computational similarity using four 384-dimensional multilingual MiniLM representations of 7,891 K-pop songs by 1,456 artists from charts spanning 2000 to October 2023. Whole-song truncated embeddings provide the strongest standardized separation between neighbouring and random song pairs (1.995), compared with 1.931 for chunked documents, although chunked representations show greater adjusted Rand agreement and line-based representations yield higher modularity. Using whole-song embeddings, we construct a weighted cosine nearest-neighbour graph ($k=30$). A representative Louvain partition identifies 21 operational communities, without a corresponding robust plateau in the Markov Stability analysis. AI-assisted examination of selected lyrics and terms suggests overlapping patterns of memory, separation, longing, self-reflection, attraction, and performance. Community membership is associated with character-script composition (Cram\'er's $V=0.294$; permutation $p=0.001$). High-participation songs exhibit broader cross-community connectivity, while participation has weak negative associations with embedding-relative novelty. These findings show how representation choices and textual characteristics influence the network organization of a cultural corpus, subject to limitations from truncation, graph construction, and the absence of independent human semantic validation.

articles.title: Draft-Thinking: Learning Efficient Reasoning in Long Chain-of-Thought LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.00578v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought~(CoT) reasoning improves the problem-solving capability of large reasoning models~(LRMs), but often incurs substantial inference cost and overthinking. Existing efficiency methods primarily rely on prompting, post-hoc compression, or length-regularized optimization; these approaches can be sensitive to model scale, depend on external estimators, or under-allocate reasoning to difficult instances. We propose \textbf{Draft-Thinking}, a lightweight adaptation framework that learns a \textit{model-adapted draft CoT}: a compact, self-contained working derivation that directly supports the final answer. We identify a \textbf{Cross-Scale Draft Mismatch}: concise traces generated by a strong teacher can be too sparse for a smaller target model. To address this mismatch, \textbf{Progressive Draft Adaptation} first transfers a concise reasoning-form prior through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and then applies two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) with progressively harder data and relaxed response budgets to calibrate the reasoning granularity to the target model.
